data.why: A street-side build in section: a block stack sinks beside the open cut, then piles, a mat and a rising steel tower show how a skyscraper really stands. The tower rig is shortened (floors 3.4 m, walls 13.6 m, spire shorter) so no panel exceeds 16 m and the whole rig stays under 18 m. The camera uses boxes to frame the deep foundation and then the full tower.

ideas.idea: stacking floors on a sidewalk looks like a skyscraper, but it is only a pile of blocks
all that weight sinks into the soft ground and the stack leans over
dig a pit and drive concrete piles down through the soft soil to solid rock
pour a thick concrete mat across the pile tops so the load spreads over all of them
the piles plus the mat are called a piled raft foundation
steel columns rise floor by floor and the piles pass the weight down to the rock
a tall, slim tower catches the wind like a sail and sways
a giant steel weight hung near the top swings against the sway and calms it
people think the thick walls hold the building up, but take the walls away and the frame still stands
the steel skeleton carries the load, an idea first used in Chicago in 1885
add glass walls, a spire and entrance steps to complete the tower
a finished tower stands calm on its deep foundation

chain.shows: the stack sinks into the ground and tilts over
chain.stakes: the whole tower would topple on the street

chain.shows: the finished frame leans and sways in the wind
chain.stakes: people inside would feel sick and the frame could be damaged

surprises.claim: The Burj Khalifa stands on 192 concrete piles, each about 1.5 m wide and 43 m long, under a 3.7 m thick concrete mat

surprises.claim: Taipei 101 hangs a steel ball damper of about 660 tonnes near the top to cut the sway in wind
The Home Insurance Building in Chicago, finished in 1885, is often called the first skyscraper because it used a steel and iron skeleton
